        "content": "Signal Processing 161 (2019) 203–213 Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Signal Processing journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/sigpro Direct position determination of multiple coherent sources using an iterative adaptive approach Tao Zhou, Wei Yi∗, Lingjiang Kong School of Information and Communication Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, 611731, China article info Article history: Received 27 June 2018 Revised 18 February 2019 Accepted 28 March 2019 Available online 29 March 2019 Keywords: Direct position determination Coherent signals Iterative adaptive approach Position extraction abstract The direct position determination (DPD) approach is known to outperform the two-step localization at low signal to noise ratio, however, and it encounters many difficulties when locating multiple coherent sources. Introduction Localization of sources is a crucial fundamental task in many application fields such as radar, sonar, navigation system and wireless sensor network, and recently attracts much interest of many researchers [1–9]. Generally, localization methods are mainly categorized as two-step localization and one-step localization. In the two-step localization method, the estimation of a source position is implemented by two processing steps, where sensors firstly measure angles or ranges of the source from received signals, such as angle of arrival (AOA), time of arrival (TOA) and time difference of arrival (TDOA), and then estimate the source position by utilizing the previous measurements according to the geometric relationship between the source and sensors [6,10–15]. In the one-step localization method, the position is determined by directly handling the raw received signals without estimating the intermediate measurements like TDOA, etc. On the basis of knowing a received signal model, the one-step localization is generally accomplished by adopting the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation [8,9,16], the least square (LS) approach [17–19] or the sparsity recovery method [20,21]. ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: tozhoutao@163.com (T. Zhou), kussoyi@gmail.com (W. Yi), lingjiang.kong@gmail.com (L. Kong). The one-step localization method can directly estimate the source position from the raw received signals, and obtain processing gain, so it has an advantage of high-accurate and robust localization over the two-step approach, especially in strong noise environment. In [17], the direct position determination (DPD) approach, belonging to the one-step localization, has shown better accuracy than the two-step localization based on AOA or TOA at low signal to noise ratio (SNR) for a single emitter. Additionally, the DPD approach has also natural superiority in application of multitarget localization, since it needn’t match these AOAs, TOAs or TDOAs to the corresponding targets as the two-step approach does. Having the advantages over the two-step localization, the DPD approach has been applied in the scene of multiple sources [18,19,22]. The DPD approach based on the multiple signal classification (MUSIC) [23], called as DPD-MUSIC, is proposed to locate multiple sources on the condition of knowing the number of sources [18]. DPD-MUSIC only requires two-dimensional spectrum peak search in a planar geometry to determine the positions of all sources without high computational cost. In [19], the high-accurate DPD combined with the minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) [24], called as DPD-MVDR, is developed to deal with the case where the number of sources are unknown. Similar with DPDMUSIC, DPD-MVDR can also locate the source positions only by two-dimensional search. But, only when the transmitted signals https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sigpro.2019.03.023 0165-1684/© 2019 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 204 T. Zhou, W. Yi and L. Kong / Signal Processing 161 (2019) 203–213 are uncorrelated or partially correlated, can both DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR obtain high localization accuracy for each source. In practice, many perfectly correlated (coherent) signals appear in some cases, such as coherent interference, multipath propagation and coherent radiation sources. In the coherent case, many techniques based on eigenstructure and beamforming, like MUSIC and MVDR approaches, fail to work [25]. Due to the property of MUSIC and MVDR, DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR will encounter a serious performance deterioration for coherent signals. Although many algorithms based on the spatial smoothing preprocessing scheme and the iterative approach have been proposed to settle the coherent signal problems [26–31], they can only provide the intermediate measurements AOAs to determine the source positions by the two-step localization [32–35]. As mentioned above, the two-step localization methods based AOA confront unstable performance at low SNR, and also have to match measurement parameters in multiple sources scene. The focus of this paper is to solve the direct localization problem of multiple coherent sources. Our proposed method combines the DPD technique with the iterative adaptive approach (IAA) [30] to estimate the positions of coherent sources. In this paper, we quantitatively analyze the reasons of invalidity of DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR for coherent signals. To avoid the covariance matrix becoming rank-deficient, we propose to employ the IAA to compute it, instead of the traditional array processing. Meanwhile, the received signals are also estimated iteratively. Based on these signals, a spatial power function is derived to compute the intercepted power from which the source positions can be determined by grid search. In addition, an extraction method based on connected domain separation is proposed to obtain the position of each source. Similar with DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR method, the proposed algorithm also requires only two-dimensional search for planar geometry to locate all sources. Unlike the two-step methods, the proposed algorithm is direct without estimating the intermediate measurements. The simulation results are shown to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm for coherent sources. The contributions of our paper are summarized as follow. (1) We propose to employ the IAA to address the direct localization problem of multiple coherent sources. The IAA is developed to apply in the one-step localization without estimating intermediate measurements AOAs. (2) For the position extraction problem that the multi-target localization always encounters, we propose a method based on connected domain separation to obtain the position of each source. The paper is organized as follows: Sections 2 and 3 state the signal model and the DPD problem formulated for coherent sources at distributed receivers, respectively. Section Sections 4 presents the proposed algorithm in detail, followed by numerical examples in Sections 5. Finally, a conclusion is drawn in Sections 6. 2. Signal model Consider a localization system consisting of L widely distributed receivers, each of which equips a M-element antenna array. It is required that K emitters (or sources) transmitting unknown coherent signals are located by the L receivers, shown in Fig. 1. The receivers and emitters are located in a two-dimensional plane. The coordinates of L receivers and K emitters are denoted by ql = (xl, yl ), l = 1,..., L and pk = (xk, yk ), k = 1,..., K, respectively. The transmitted signals from K emitters, represented by sk(t ), k = 1,..., K, are unknown to the receivers and assumed to be coherent [36], i.e, sk(t ) = βks0(t ), k = 1,..., K, (1) Fig. 1. The central processors process the signals from many distributed receivers to locate the emitters. where s0(t) is a common waveform of the transmitted signals and the complex constant βk contains the information of phase and amplitude of the transmitted signals. Obviously, the signals are perfectly correlated due to only having the difference of initial phase and amplitude. Assume that each receiver can intercept signals of all emitters during the observation interval when the emitters are regarded to be stationary. The received signal at receiver l can be expressed as rl (t ) = K ∑ k=1 αlkal (pk )sk(t − τl (pk )) + el (t ), 0 ≤ t ≤ T, (2) where αlk is an unknown complex attenuation coefficient corresponding to the direct path from the emitter k to the receiver l, mutually independent, and al(pk) represents the array response of the receiver l to the emitter k. The term el(t) stands for noise and interference received by the lth array, including weak multipath [17]. They are assumed to be independent at different antenna elements and receivers. It is worth noting that the single-path model above is inappropriate for those scenes of dense multipath [37]. The propagation time of the signal from the emitter k to the receiver l is computed by τl (pk ) = ‖ql − pk‖ c, (3) where c is the speed of light and ‖ · ‖ represents the Euclidean norm. We equally partition the observed signal time T into N segments, where N is seen as the number of samples. Assume that T is enough long for the region of interest such that T/N max l,k {τl (pk )} [18]. The Fourier transformation coefficients of the nth (n = 1,..., N) segment from the received signal rl(t) are approximately denoted by [18,19] rl (ωi, n) = K ∑ k=1 αlke− jωiτl (pk)al (pk )sk(ωi, n) + el (ωi, n), (4) where rl(ωi, n), sk(ωi, n) and el(ωi, n) represent the Fourier coefficients of rl(t), sk(t) and el(t) from the nth segment at frequency ωi, i = 1,..., I, respectively. Note that the Fourier coefficients of the transmitted signals, sk(ωi, n) = βks0(ωi, n), k = 1,..., K, still remain coherent in frequency domain, where s0(ωi, n) is the Fourier coefficient of s0(t). As shown in (4), the position parameter of the emitter is decoupled from the signal sk(t − τl (pk )) by the Fourier transformation. Define  ̃al (pk, ωi ) = e− jωiτl (pk)al (pk ), (5)\n\n\nT. Zhou, W. Problem formulation about direct position determination of coherent sources As denoted in (6), the position parameters of the emitters only appear at the equivalent array response a ̃l (pk, ωi ), so many spectral methods can be employed to estimate the positions [18,19]. For brevity, (6) is rewritten as the vector form rl (ωi, n) = Al (θ, ωi)s(ωi, n) + el (ωi, n), (7) where Al (θ, ωi ) = [αl1  ̃al (p1, ωi ),..., αlK  ̃al (pK, ωi )], s(ωi, n) = [s1(ωi, n),..., sK (ωi, n)], and “ ” is the transpose notation. Considering the coherency defined in (1), the correlation matrix of the transmitted signals in frequency domain can be expressed as E{s(ωi)sH (ωi)} = ββHE{|s0(ωi)|2}, (8) where β = [β1,..., βK ] and ( · )H denotes the conjugate transpose. Note that the rank of E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} is equal to 1. The coherency exactly reflects on the correlation matrix. It is also worth mentioning that if the transmitting signals were noncoherent, there would be no signals satisfying sk′ (ωi, n) = βsk(ωi, n) for any k′ = k, where β is a complex constant. It means that the correlation matrix E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} could always keep its rank full. In [18], according to DPD-MUSIC algorithm, all received signals of L receivers are assembled at a central processing unit, written in a simplified form as follows: r(ωi, n) = A(θ, ωi)s(ωi, n) + e(ωi, n), (9) where r(ωi, n) = [r1 (ωi, n),..., rL (ωi, n)], e(ωi, n) = [e1 (ωi, n),..., eL (ωi, n)], A(θ, ωi) = [A1 (θ, ωi),..., AL (θ, ωi)], θ = [p1,..., pK ]. When using the MUSIC approach, the covariance matrix of the received signal r(ωi, n) is required to be computed. That is R(ωi) = E{r(ωi)rH (ωi)} = A(θ, ωi)E{s(ωi)sH (ωi)}AH (θ, ωi) + ηI, (10) where ηI is the covariance matrix related to noise part. Note that as shown in (8), the rank of E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} is much less than the number of signals K, which can result in the rank-deficient property of R(ωi). DPD-MUSIC algorithm is implemented on the basis of the orthogonality of signal subspace and noise subspace, so it needs to make an eigenvalue decomposition for the covariance matrix R(ωi). However, affected by the rank-deficient covariance matrix R(ωi), only the eigenvectors less than the number of emitters can be obtained. Therefore, it leads to the invalidation of DPD-MUSIC algorithm for coherent signals. The similar consequence also happens in the DPD-MVDR algorithm [19], since the inverse of the covariance matrix is required to be computed when using MVDR approach. The rank-deficient property of the covariance matrix also significantly causes unstable computation of its inverse, which further results in the degradation of the robustness and accuracy of DPD-MVDR for the coherent sources. Next, we will focus our attention on the solution to locate multiple coherent sources. 4. Direct position determination algorithm of multiple coherent sources In this section, the DPD based on the IAA is derived to solve the localization problem for the coherent sources, called as DPD-IAA below for brevity. DPD-IAA utilizes signal power to estimate the source positions essentially. We first employ the weighted least square (WLS) to estimate the intercepted signals, and then further compute the covariance matrix and the spatial power iteratively by the estimated signals. After determining the convergent spatial power function, the positions of each source is extracted from it by a connected domain separation method. The DPD-IAA algorithm mainly consists of three parts: estimation of the intercepted signals, iterative computation of the spatial power function and extraction of multiple source positions. 4.1. Estimation of the intercepted signals All received signals are transmitted to a central processor to compute the positions of emitters. Let s ̃lk(ωi, n) = αlksk(ωi, n), and the signal model shown in (6) can be rewritten as rl (ωi, n) = K ∑ k=1  ̃al (pk, ωi )s ̃lk(ωi, n) + el (ωi, n), (11) where s ̃lk(ωi, n) can be regarded as the kth transmitted signal modulated by path loss from the emitter k to the receiver l, also called as the intercepted signal. So the average power that the receiver l intercepts from the emitter k at frequency ωi over observation time T can be expressed as P(l) k (ωi) = 1 T N ∑ n=1 |s ̃lk(ωi, n)|2, (12) where N denotes the number of frequency signal samples during the observation. In order to estimate the intercepted signals, we need to consider each position in the surveillance region because of not knowing the signals. Here, denote the two-dimensional region by Θ ⊆ R2. For the position of interest pk ∈ Θ (pk may also not include a source), according to the signal model in (11), an interference and noise covariance matrix at frequency ωi from the receiver l is defined by Ql (pk, ωi ) = Rl (ωi ) − P(l) k (ωi ) ̃al (pk, ωi ) ̃aH l (pk, ωi ), (13) where Rl(ωi) characterizes the covariance matrix of the received signals, defined as Rl (ωi) Al (Θ, ωi)Pl (ωi)AH l (Θ, ωi). Iterative computation of the spatial power function In this subsection, we define a spatial power function to determine the source positions, where an iterative method is employed to compute the covariance matrix and the spatial power. An algorithm procedure based on grid search is provided to achieve the localization of coherent sources. Let P(pk) represent the sum of the power that all receivers intercept from the position pk, and the spatial power function is given by P(pk) = 1 2π L ∑ l=1 I ∑ i=1 Pˆ(l)(ωi, pk ), (22) where Pˆ(l)(ωi, pk ) denotes the estimated power of the position pk at the frequency ωi from the receiver l, computed by (12). According to the definition of the spatial power function, we can see that the position containing an emitter has a larger value than the ones not containing emitters because of collecting more signal energy. If the received signals come from K emitters, K peaks will appear at the spatial power function P(pk). Therefore, once obtaining the estimates of s ̃lk(ωi, n) from all receivers, we can determine the positions of the emitters by finding the peak values of the spatial power function in the entire region. Combing (12) with (22), the position estimates of the emitters can be obtained by pˆ k = arg mpax 1 2π T ∑L l=1 I ∑ i=1 N ∑ n=1  ̃aH l (p, ωi )R−1 l (ωi)rl (ωi, n)  ̃aH l (p, ωi )R−1 l (ωi ) ̃al (p, ωi ). (23) However, computing the spatial power function in (22) involves the inverse of covariance matrix Rl(ωi). If Rl(ωi) is calculated by the approach directly based on snapshots as done in DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR algorithms, shown in (10), it will inevitably cause Rl(ωi) to become rank-deficient. Instead of the traditional methods, we utilize the iterative approach in [30] to compute R−1 l (ωi ), which relies on the estimated signal of the previous iteration but not on the received snapshots in (11). As indicated in (14) and (12), Rl(ωi) can be deter mined by the power P(l) k (ωi ) of the estimated signal ˆs ̃lk(pk, ωi, n), rather than E{rl (ωi, n)rH l (ωi, n)}. Meanwhile, as shown in (21), ˆs ̃lk(pk, ωi, n) is also related to Rl(ωi), so the computation of Rl(ωi) can be implemented iteratively. The initialization of P(l) k (ωi ) is done by Pˆ(l ) k (ωi) = ∑N n=1 |  ̃aH l (pk, ωi)rl (ωi, n)|2 N|  ̃aH l (pk, ωi ) ̃al (pk, ωi )|2, pk ∈ Θ. (24) Such iterative approach based on (12), (14) and (21) can effectively avoid the singularity of Rl(ωi). As referred in [30], only a few iterations are required when the algorithm is convergent. After such iterative computation, the estimated signal can be also determined. It should be noted that the approach also can handle the case of noncoherent signals due to not demanding any assumption about the correlation property of the signals, which is shown in the numerical experiment of the later section. Once attaining the estimated signals ˆs ̃lk(pk, ωi, n) at scanning grids, we can calculate the spatial power of the entire region of interest by (22), and further determine the positions of the K emitters only by twodimensional search for the spatial power function. An algorithm procedure based on grid search is displayed in Algorithm 1. 4.3. Extraction of multiple source positions We have derived the spatial power function about the positions so far. However, in the multi-target localization algorithms based on grid search, such as DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR, the source positions require to be extracted from the objective function, equivalent to the spatial power function in the DPD-IAA. This subsection mainly introduces a method based on connected domain separation to extract the position of each source from the spatial power function. As referred in the previous subsection, the K peaks will appear in the region of search when K emitters exist. Fig. 2(a) shows the spatial power map containing three emitters, computed by (22). In this map, brighter the yellow color is, larger the power value is. The areas in which the true emitters are located have brighter yellow than the others. However, since numerous local maximum values exist in the spatial power function, the position of each emitter is difficult to obtain directly from it by search of peak values. For this problem, we adopt the method combing threshold processing with connected domain separation to extract the positions. Firstly, we determine a threshold according to the spatial power function, given by λT = χ mpax P(p), (25) where 0 < χ 1, and the threshold is set to the χ times maximum value of the spatial power function. χ is selected according\n\n\nT. The initial threshold is generally selected to approach or equal the maximum value of the power function, namely χ close to 1. It is seen next that choosing a smaller χ means obtaining more separate connected domains. The threshold processing is aimed at obtaining the separate areas containing emitters. Fig. 2(b) shows the spatial power map over the threshold of χ = 0.9. Only one emitter is located in this map, and its position can be obtained easily by finding the maximum value. Secondly, turn down the threshold with a step λT, and we can get more separate connected domains, denoted by Ω1,..., ΩD, D 1. We utilize the connected domain separation approach to isolate the areas and extract the position of each emitter from them respectively. To determine the positions of all emitters, we still need to continue lowering the threshold to obtain more separate connected domains. As shown in Fig. 2(d), all three emitters appear in three different separated domains, where their positions can be extracted respectively. The extraction algorithm does not stop working until the number of all extracted emitters equals to the true one. The number of the emitters can be detected by the MDL principle [28]. The detailed procedures are provided in Algorithm 2. 5. Numerical examples In this section, we investigate the proposed DPD-IAA, DPDMUSIC and DPD-MVDR algorithms for multiple sources in the two situations of transmitting coherent and noncoherent signals. The Monte Carlo simulation experiments are conducted to examine the performance of three algorithms. In each of the experiments, three sources are distributed randomly at three different rectangular regions respectively with their centers located at coordinates (−8, 12) km, (0,18) km and (8,12) km while four receivers remain unchanged at coordinates (−10, 0) km, (−5, −5) km, (5, −5) km and (10,0) km, as illustrated in Fig. 3. Considering the invalidity of the above localization algorithms at very low SNR, an effective estimate rate (EER) is defined to describe how many times the estimated source positions are located inside the specified range of a true position in all experiments, and computed by EER = Ne Nt, (26) where Nt is the total number of all experiments and Ne stands for the number of the experiments in which the estimated position lies in the specified range of the true one. Based on that a source can be estimated effectively, the root mean square error (RMSE) is chosen to evaluate localization accuracy of the algorithms, 208 T. Zhou, W. Yi and L. Algorithm 2: The Extraction Algorithm of the Source Positions. In the simulation experiments, every receiver is equipped with a uniform linear array consisting of 10 antenna elements spaced at the half-wavelength distance. Noise received by the antennas follows a circular complex Gaussian distribution with zero mean and standard deviation of 1. The phases of attenuation coefficients follow the uniform distribution at [−π, π ] and are independent mutually in each experiment. Their amplitudes are generally described by the intensity of received signals and can be determined by SNR. Each simulation experiment is implemented on the basis of 5 snapshots at a single frequency (i.e., N = 5, i = 1). The initial thresholds of the three algorithms are set 0.9 times of the maximum values of the respective objective functions. After each extracting the source positions, the threshold decreases with the step 0.1 times of the maximum value. 5.1. The localization performance for coherent sources In order to check the effectiveness of the proposed DPD-IAA algorithm for coherent sources, we firstly investigate the case that all transmitted signals are coherent. It means that the signals are identical except for their initial phases and amplitudes. Convenient for verifying the performance of the algorithms, we consider the complex single frequency signals with same frequency and different initial phases. The frequency snapshots of each receiver are complex constants with fixed phases and are perfectly correlated. Fig. 4 indicates the objective function maps of three algorithms over a plane at 10dB SNR from a single experiment. In the maps, brighter yellow color corresponds to a larger objective function value. Affected by the rank-deficient covariance matrix of the received signals, both DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR algorithms fail to locate accurately all three sources, as shown in Fig. 4(b) and (c) where only two true sources lie on the areas having larger function values. Compared with both DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR, the DPD-IAA can obtain three peaks containing all sources in the spatial power map, as shown in Fig. 4(a), which means that it has the capability to cope with the localization of multiple coherent sources. The source positions can be extracted from the three largest peak values in the objective function map. To further validate the performance of the proposed algorithm, we examine the localization accuracy of three algorithms by conducting 500 independent experiments at different SNRs. In each experiment, the method based on the connected domain separation is adopted to extract the position of each source from the objective function map. The localization performance for noncoherent sources In order to examine the ability of DPD-IAA algorithm to locate multiple noncoherent sources, we select random flat narrowband Gaussian signals as the transmitted signals and also compare the performance of three algorithms for each source. Similarly, the EER and RMSE are still chosen to evaluate the performance of the algorithms. Fig. 8 shows the EERs and RMSEs of the three algorithms for each source, respectively. As is expected, both DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR display the great localization performance for the noncoherent sources. Including DPD-IAA, the EER curves of three algorithms for each source have the same trend of converging to 1 at high SNR while their RMSEs also decrease smoothly with SNR rising. DPD-IAA algorithm almost has an excellent localization performance like DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR. It is worthy of mentioning that the little EER performance loss of DPD-IAA at low SNR, shown in Fig. 8(a), (c) and (e), is because the iterative approach is more sensitive to the larger noise than the method directly based on the snapshots when computing the covariance. For a specified number of the elements, both EER and RMSE are computed on basis of 500 independent experiments. Fig. 9(a) and (b) show the curves of EER and RMSE at 0 dB SNR with respect to the number of antenna elements, ranging from 2 to 20, respectively. It is seen from the Fig. 9(a) that the EER is kept at a lower level when only fewer elements are used for localization. With the elements increasing, the EER rises continually and converges to 1 eventually. On the other hand, the RMSE continues to fall, as shown in Fig. 9(b). It is because processing signals by an array has functions of accumulating signal energy and forming spatial beamwidth. More antennas can offer higher gain and narrower beamwidth, which helps improve the localization performance. Higher gain allows locating sources at lower SNR while narrower beamwidth has the ability to resolve adjacent sources more easily. Therefore, based on demand, we can select an appropriate number of antenna elements to locate sources in practical application. 6. Conclusion In this paper, we propose the localization algorithm combining the IAA method with the DPD concept to locate multiple coherent sources with distributed receivers. The paper derives the spatial power function to estimate the source positions. The proposed algorithm can still work effectively even though the signals are perfectly correlated. The method based on connected domain separation is also proposed to extract the position of each source. Simulation experiments compare the performance of the proposed algorithm with the existing DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR algorithms. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm can locate each of coherent sources accurately while the other algorithms fail to cope with localization of coherent sources. Additionally, the proposed algorithm can achieve the same excellent localization performance with both DPD-MUSIC and DPD-MVDR algorithms for the noncoherent signals. The effects of the number of antennas on the proposed algorithm are also investigated by the numerical experiment. This paper only considers the case where the received signals are dominated by a direct path. For more complicated scenes where multipath is not negligible, our future work will focus on the direct localization issue of multiple coherent sources in this case. Conflict of interest None.
